An open ISA is remarkably interesting for space due to several reasons: It reduces potential difficulties in license negotiation or export restrictions. It allows to perform modifications for radiation mitigation. It adds or modifies instructions to execute functions that are frequently required by space applications, such as bit manipulation, sub-word arithmetic, vector or SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) computations.RISC-V has been gaining popularity in the past years, and its use in space is now close to a reality thanks to several on-going system-on-chip (SoC) developments that will embed RISC-V multi core processor, along with several other interfaces to enable their use in satellite payloads and platforms, such as SpaceFibre, TM/TC (telemetry/telecommand) or cryptographic functions. The successful adoption of this architecture and embarking of the future SoC depends in a great extent on the features of the hardware, and on the availability of software development tool chains that enable the programming of the cores with suitable on-board software.Hardware and software developments around RISC-V can benefit greatly from the hardware-software co-design development flow, which simultaneously considers hardware and software within the design process. This enables the co-development and co-verification of hardware and software using simulation and/or emulation with the help of tools such as virtual platforms where simulation models of the processor ISA, and models of other components of the SoC can be executed at different levelsof abstraction, and with the required simulation speed. A fast ISA simulator of RISC-V facilitates early software development and the development software tool chains. All this before the first hardware prototypes are available.ESA has promoted the development of the SoCRocket virtual platform, which has been made available to missions and projects. This platform is comprised by several functional blocks, and can be used to simulate a SoC, but now, only LEON based systems are currently supported.This activity aims at developing a simulation model of RISC-V that can be executed in a suitable virtual platform at an appropriate abstraction level, easing the development of software, and enabling hardware-software co-design and design space exploration of a system-on-chip.The main tasks to be accomplished are: Assess the suitability of a virtual platform to simulate a RISC-V based SoC considering trade-offs related to accuracy of the models and simulation speed, SoCRocket and possible alternatives. Create a simulation model of the RISC-Vinstruction set, that can be integrated in a virtual platform, directly or through an emulator, and aid the development of software. Develop and integrate new functional blocks in a virtual platform, such as: SpaceFibre, TM/TC functions, cryptography, Ethernet.
